newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Foreign investment in Pakistan stocks seen rising.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investment in Pakistan stocks seen rising.

text.p: Foreign investors are showing renewed interest in Pakistani stocks, but political and economic stability is vital to sustain the trend, the president of the Karachi Stock Exchange said on Monday.
"If Pakistan gets political stability as the result of the coming elections and IMF-backed economic measures are fully implemented, the economy can revive," Arif Habib told Reuters.

Pakistanis go to the polls on February 3 in national and provincial elections ordered by President Farooq Leghari after he sacked Benazir Bhutto's government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
Habib said selected scrips had attracted some New Year buying by foreigners lured by their low prices relative to other markets in the region.
He said expectations of a turn-around in textile stocks had been boosted by the caretaker government's incentives for the sector, and several firms had announced good results.
"A number of companies have come out with cash dividends which would improve the liquidity position," he added.

The Karachi bourse attracted more foreign portfolio investment in 1996 than in 1995 despite political uncertainty and economic worries, receiving a net inflow of 1.882 billion rupees ($46.79 million), up from 242 million rupees.
There was a total inflow of 8.839 billion rupees in 1996 against an outflow of 6.957 billion rupees.
Portfolio investment inflows outpaced outflows in the first half, but a tax-packed budget for 1996/97 (July-June) and growing political instability upset the trend, Habib said.

"Our market had attracted foreign invesments in 1996 which constituted almost 12.5 percent of the holdings. The main problem was the weakness of the local financial institutions, which remained sellers throughout the year," he said.
Foreign investors siphoned 7.362 billion rupees out of the Pakistani market in the second half of the year.

Ather Raouf, an analyst at Carr Mashriq, said an improved cotton crop had created hopes at the beginning of last year that Pakistan's exports would revive and the balance of payments and foreign exchange reserves position would improve.
The 100-share index soared to its year-high of 1,855.22 points on February 15 from 1,470.87 on January 1. The index stayed above 1,700 until the budget was announced in June.
Raouf said the government had opted to impose fresh taxes on already heavily-taxed sectors to try to meet its aim of reducing the budget deficit to four percent of Gross Domestic Product.
The economic outlook worsened in the second half when the cotton crop proved disappointing, foreign reserves slumped and the government ran into debt servicing problems.
The index dropped to a year-low of 1,332.14 on September 10 and by year-end had recovered only to 1,339 points.
